## Symmetric MultiZenoTravel {#sec-front}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Proposition I: the Pareto front is reached with exactly 2t − p central cities
:::

The method to find the Pareto Front of any general MultiZenoTravel instance consists of three
steps. First, we provide an efficient algorithm to find the Pareto Front for any symmetric clique
MultiZenoTravel instance. Then, we show that for the non-symmetric version of the problem the
method still applies when flights between central cities are not shorter than a detour through
$C_I$ or $C_G$, provided waiting is accounted for, and that the extension to shorter flights
proposed in the 2023 version of this paper misses the front. Last, we study the transformation of
any instance of the general MultiZenoTravel problem into a non-symmetric clique version, and show
that it does not preserve the Pareto front in general. This section covers the first step; it
corresponds to §2 to §4 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md).

The following proposition is the cornerstone of the method to identify and construct the Pareto
Set of any instance:

::: {.statement}
**Proposition I**: Assume (S) and (H), in particular (S) and (AΔ), or (S) and (A1). Every point of
the Pareto front is attained by a plan where exactly $2t - p$ (possibly identical) central cities
are used by a plane.
:::

Proposition I is {{< node "Theorem 4.5" >}} together with {{< node "Theorem 4.1" >}}: every point
of the front is the point of an admissible partition of $2t - p$ landings, which Theorem 4.1 flies
with exactly these landings. (A1) and (AΔ) imply (H) by Lemma 1.5.

By Corollary II, no plan performs fewer than $2t - p$ patterns, so Proposition I reduces the
search to lists of $2t - p$ cities. It is a statement about the front: a Pareto-optimal plan may
land more often. [[QS15](#ref-QS15)] and the 2023 version of this paper state Proposition I for
every Pareto-optimal plan; it holds only in the form above.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Example 4.6" >}} **An optimal plan with extra landings.** Take $n = 1$,
$d_1 = \bar d_1 = 1$, $c_1 = 0$, $t = 5$ and $p = 3$, so $2t - p = 7$, with any flight between
central cities. The front is $\{(0, 6)\}$, and a feasible plan with 9 central landings attains
$(0, 6)$: every plane flies $C_I \to C_1 \to C_G \to C_1 \to C_I \to C_1 \to C_G$ from time 0,
without waiting; planes 2 and 3 carry a passenger on both patterns $A$, plane 1 on its first only.
:::

The goal of this section is to establish the proof of Proposition I for the Symmetric case. For
that purpose, we first describe which lists of $2t - p$ cities can be flown, and how fast. We then
show that every plan is dominated by one of them under the hub triangles (H), which both the
assumption (A1) of [[QS15](#ref-QS15)] and the triangular inequality (AΔ) imply. Precisely, with
$$M(X) = \min\Big\{\max_k \ell(X_k) : X_1, \dots, X_p \text{ an admissible partition of } X\Big\},$$
the front is the Pareto set of the pairs $(c(X), M(X))$ over the lists $X$ of $2t - p$ cities that
have an admissible partition.

### Admissible partitions {#sec-admissible}

A list of $2t - p$ cities does not hold any information about which plane will land in a
particular city. Assign to each plane $k$ the cities $X_k$ in which it lands: when can the
partition $X_1, \dots, X_p$ be flown with simple patterns? By Lemma 3.1, a plane performs one
more $A$ than $\bar A$, so a plane that performs only those patterns lands an odd number of times.
A plane that lands an even number of times has to perform a pattern $B$ or $\bar B$, that is, to
leave a passenger in a central city for another plane, or to take one left there by another
plane. These hand-offs pair up at each city. Admissibility records exactly this bookkeeping,
modulo 2.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition 2.1" >}} **Admissible partition.** A *parity matrix* for $X_1, \dots, X_p$
is a matrix $h \in \{0, 1\}^{p \times n}$ such that

* (h1) $h_{k,i} = 1$ implies $X_k(i) \ge 1$;
* (h2) $\sum_i h_{k,i} \equiv |X_k| + 1 \pmod 2$ for every plane $k$;
* (h3) $\sum_k h_{k,i} \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ for every city $i$.

The partition is *admissible* if it has a parity matrix.
:::

Here $h_{k,i} = 1$ means that plane $k$ takes part in an odd number of hand-offs in city $i$.
(h2) asks a plane with an even group, an *even plane*, to do so in an odd number of cities, and
(h3) pairs the hand-offs of every city. In graph terms, the marked pairs $(k, i)$ are a
$\mathcal T$-join, for the set $\mathcal T$ of even planes, of the bipartite graph $H$ on planes and
cities with an edge between $k$ and $i$ whenever $X_k(i) \ge 1$. Counting with multiplicities
changes nothing: integer entries $0 \le \tilde h_{k,i} \le X_k(i)$ with the parities of (h2) and
(h3) exist if and only if a parity matrix does ({{< node "Lemma 2.2" >}}).

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 2.4" >}} **Row bound.** For every parity matrix and plane $k$,
$\sum_i h_{k,i} + 1 \le |X_k|$. Hence the groups of an admissible partition are non-empty, and
$|X| \equiv p \pmod 2$.
:::

The condition reads more simply when no two groups share a city.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 2.3" >}} **Disjoint groups.** If no city lies in two groups, the partition is
admissible if and only if every group has odd size.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Odd groups have the zero matrix as a parity matrix. Conversely, a city that lies in one
group is marked in at most one row, hence by (h3) in none, and (h2) makes every group odd
({{< node "Lemma 2.3" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

On the [example instance](#fig-plan), the groups $\{2, 3\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$ are admissible: both
planes are even, and marking $C_2$ in both rows gives a parity matrix. The groups $\{1, 1\}$ and
$\{3, 3\}$ are not: each plane is even, but they share no city, so each would have to hand a
passenger to a plane that never comes to its city. Odd groups, such as $\{1\}$ and $\{1, 1, 1\}$,
are always admissible: the zero matrix is a parity matrix.

### (BB̄)-pairings and link forests {#sec-links}

A *($B\bar B$)-pairing* in city $i$ is a pattern $B$ of one plane and a pattern $\bar B$ of
another plane, both in $i$, carrying the same passenger: the first plane leaves it in $i$, the
second takes it to $C_G$. The parity matrix says in which cities the pairings are, but not between
which planes. A link forest says both.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition 2.5" >}} A *link forest* for $X_1, \dots, X_p$ is a forest $\Lambda$ of
rooted trees on the planes whose edges, the *links*, carry city labels. The group of a plane
consists of its *free landings*, one landing in the label of each link to a child, and one landing
in the label of the link to its parent, so that

* (F1) the links at a plane $u$ use distinct landings of its group: for every city $i$, at most
  $X_u(i)$ links at $u$ are labelled $i$;
* (F2) every plane $u$ has an odd number $r_u = |X_u| - \deg_\Lambda(u)$ of free landings.

A link between $u$ and $v$ labelled $i$, a *link* in $i$, is a $(B\bar B)$-pairing; the $r_u$
free landings of $u$ are performed as patterns $A, \bar A, \dots, A$.
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 2.6" >}} **Link forest.** A partition is admissible if and only if it has a link
forest.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Counting the labels of a link forest at each plane gives an integer parity matrix
({{< node "Lemma 2.2" >}}). Conversely, a parity matrix with the fewest marks has no cycle, so
some plane is marked in no city, and is a tree of its own, or in exactly one city $i$; removing it,
with one landing in $i$ of another plane marked in $i$, leaves a smaller admissible partition, and
the plane hangs back by a link in $i$, by induction
({{< node "Lemma 2.6" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

### Constructing the plan {#sec-achievability}

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 4.1" >}} Assume (S) and $p \le t$. For every table of flights between central
cities, every admissible partition $X_1, \dots, X_p$ of a list $X$ of $2t - p$ cities is flown by a
feasible plan whose planes land exactly at the groups, up to relabelling the planes, so of cost
$c(X)$, and whose makespan is $\max_k \ell(X_k)$.
:::

The construction roots every tree of a link forest at a plane. For a link in $i$ between a parent
$u$ and a child $v$, $u$ performs the pattern $B$ and $v$ the pattern $\bar B$. The western part
of each pairing is performed as early as possible, and its eastern part as late as possible: each
plane flies its patterns $B$ first, from time 0, then its free landings as patterns $A$ and
$\bar A$, then its pattern $\bar B$ if it has a parent. A plane has at most one parent, so it
performs at most one $\bar B$, at the end of its sequence. That $\bar B$ may have to wait for the
passenger, but the parent flies its patterns $B$ first, so the wait ends within the parent's own
duration, and no plane finishes later than its load or its parent's.

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* The child $v$ arrives in $i$ at $\ell(X_v) - d_i$, and the parent's drop-off arrives
there by $\tau_u - d_i$, where $\tau_u \le \ell(X_u)$ is the duration of $u$'s patterns $B$. So
$v$ is back in $C_G$ by $\max(\ell(X_v), \ell(X_u))$, and every plane flies exactly $\ell(X_k)$
({{< node "Theorem 4.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

### A lower bound for every plan {#sec-relaxation}

A first lower bound on the cost of every plan comes from forgetting admissibility. It needs a
bound on the duration of a pattern.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 3.4" >}} **Pattern durations.**

*(a)* A plane of a feasible plan has a multiset $Z$ of central cities, one per pattern, with
$2e(Z)$ at most the time it ends and $c(Z)$ at most its landing costs.

*(b)* Assume (S) and (H). Every pattern of a plane of a feasible plan lands in at least one central
city and lasts at least $2d_y$ for every central city $y$ it lands in. A chain (Lemma 3.2) ends at
least $d_y$ after any of its legs arrives in a central city $y$.

*(c)* On a route without flights between central cities, every pattern is simple, and a simple
pattern in $x$ lasts exactly $d_x + \bar d_x$ ($A$, $\bar A$), $2 d_x$ ($B$) or $2\bar d_x$
($\bar B$); the patterns of a route whose legs all arrive by $M$ last at most $M$ in total.
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 3.5" >}} **Relaxation.** Let $p \le t$. For every feasible plan with cost $C$ and
makespan $M$ there are non-empty multisets $Y_1, \dots, Y_p$ with $\sum_k |Y_k| = 2t - p$,
$c(Y_1 + \dots + Y_p) \le C$ and $2e(Y_k) \le M$ for every $k$; under (S), $e = d$, so
$\ell(Y_k) \le M$. Hence $C \ge L(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor)$, where
$$L(T) = \min\Big\{c(Y) : Y = Y_1 + \dots + Y_p,\ |Y| = 2t - p,\ Y_k \ne \emptyset \text{ and } e(Y_k) \le T \text{ for all } k\Big\}.$$
No assumption on the flights between central cities is needed.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Charge each pattern to whichever of its first and last central cities has the smaller
$e$, which by Lemma 3.4(a) costs at most half its flight time in load; by Corollary II there are
at least $2t - p$ patterns, at least one per plane, and their charged landings are distinct. Remove
landings from groups with at least two until $2t - p$ remain
({{< node "Lemma 3.5" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

$L$ is the minimisation that defines the front, without admissibility. A certificate whose gaps
are all closed by $L$ holds whatever the flights between central cities
([certificates](#sec-certificates)).

### Proof of Proposition I under the hub triangles {#sec-converse}

Under (A1), a flight between central cities can always be replaced by a detour through $C_G$:
using the same plane, the passenger on board flies to $C_G$ instead, and the plane flies on to
the next city, arriving no later. The plan then only performs simple patterns. Without (A1), the
detour through $C_G$ can be longer than the flight it replaces, so a pattern may visit several
central cities while its duration pays for only one of them. Each pattern can still be *reduced*:
by Lemma 3.4(b), under (S) and (H), a pattern lasts at least twice the duration $d_x$ of every
city $x$ it visits, so a simple pattern of the same type in any of these cities, or in a city of
smaller duration, is no longer, and lands only once. Reducing patterns one by one does not
conclude, however. After the reduction, the passenger left by a pattern $B$ may be taken by a
pattern $\bar B$ in another city, and moving both to the city of smaller duration requires two
landings there, which may cost more than the two landings they replace. The proof below does not
follow passengers at all.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 4.4" >}} **Converse under (S) and (H).** Assume (S), (H) and $p \le t$. If every
plane flies a route from $C_I$ at time 0 to $C_G$ and every passenger rides a chain
(Lemma 3.2) of legs of the plan, then some admissible partition $X_1, \dots, X_p$ of a list $X$ of
$2t - p$ cities has $c(X)$ at most the cost of the plan and $\ell(X_k) \le F_k$ for every plane. In
particular, every feasible plan with cost $C$ and makespan $M$ gives such a partition, with
$c(X) \le C$ and $\ell(X_k) \le F_k \le M$ for every $k$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* By Lemma 3.4(b), the route of every plane is a sequence of patterns, each lasting at
least twice the largest $d$ it visits. Planes that share a central city form classes, whose
parities the counting of Corollary II fixes; where a class has the wrong parity, two patterns of
one of its planes are merged. $(B\bar B)$-pairings between planes are laid along paths that join
the planes with an even number of patterns within each class, so that every plane gets the right
parity, and pairings that meet at one pattern are re-paired, each moved to the city of smaller
duration together with the landing that pays for it, until every pattern carries at most one. Each
pattern then takes one city, of duration at most the largest it visits. The pairings define an
integer parity matrix ({{< node "Lemma 2.2" badge=false >}}), and {{< node "Lemma 4.3" >}} removes
landings two at a time down to $2t - p$ ({{< node "Theorem 4.4" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

By {{< node "Lemma 1.5" badge=false >}}, the converse holds under (S) and the assumption (A1) of
[[QS15](#ref-QS15)], and under (S) and the triangular inequality (AΔ). The proof uses no timing:
only the patterns, their landings and which planes share which cities. Theorem 4.4 is
machine-checked in Lean, as `Feasible.exists_admissible_hub`, with the corollaries
`Feasible.exists_admissible_A1_flightTime` under (A1) and `Feasible.exists_admissible_ATri` under
(AΔ). Independently of the proof, the experiment [E6](#sec-e6) searched the gaps where $L$ lies
below the admissible optimum, on small instances with the shortest flights between central cities
the triangular inequality allows, and found no plan cheaper than that optimum.

With Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 1.7, this proves Proposition I, in the following precise form. The
same holds when planes may finish anywhere, as in PDDL problems without goals on the planes.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 4.5" >}} **Symmetric front.** Assume (S), (H) and $p \le t$. Let
$\mathcal P$ be the set of the points $(c(X), \max_k \ell(X_k))$ of the admissible partitions of
the lists $X$ of $2t - p$ cities, let
$$\mathcal X = \{(c(X), M(X)) : |X| = 2t - p,\ X \text{ has an admissible partition}\},$$
and let $\mathcal A'$ be the set of the points of the plans whose planes may end anywhere. Then
$$\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A' = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal P = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal X.$$
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* $\mathcal P \subseteq \mathcal A$ by Theorem 4.1, and every point of $\mathcal A$ is
weakly dominated by a point of $\mathcal P$ by Theorem 4.4, so Lemma 1.7 applies. For planes that
end anywhere, cut every route after its last leg that belongs to a chain, and complete a route that
then ends in a central city $b$ by an empty leg $b \to C_G$, which arrives by the makespan by
Lemma 3.4(b). The planes left without legs are added back one at a time by
{{< node "Lemma 4.2" >}}, which gives a new plane one city taken from the others without raising
the cost or the largest load ({{< node "Theorem 4.5" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

@tbl-example lists an admissible partition for each point of the example instance. Every point
uses two even groups and one $(B\bar B)$-pairing. Groups of sizes 1 and 3 put three landings on
one plane; $\{1\}, \{1, 1, 1\}$ for instance costs 36 with makespan 12, and is dominated by
$(24, 12)$.

Everything built on the converse holds under (S) and (H): the front as the breakpoints of a
function of the levels ({{< node "Proposition 6.3" badge=false >}}), the verified solver
({{< node "Theorem 6.9" badge=false >}}) and the `forest` gaps of a certificate
({{< node "Theorem 8.2" badge=false >}}).

### The assumption is needed {#sec-ex413}

Without (H), a plan can beat every admissible partition, so Proposition I needs some assumption on
the flights between central cities.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Example 4.7" >}} **(H) cannot be dropped.** Take $d = \bar d = (2, 3, 9, 11)$,
$c = (50, 44, 17, 0)$, $t = 6$ and $p = 3$, so $2t - p = 9$, and the symmetric flights between
central cities $d_{12} = 1$, $d_{13} = 5$, $d_{14} = 6$, $d_{23} = 3$, $d_{24} = 6$, $d_{34} = 1$
and $d_{ii} = 0$. (S) holds and (H) fails: $d_4 = 11 > d_3 + d_{34} = 10$. A feasible plan has
cost 260 and makespan 39, while every admissible partition of 9 landings with every
$\delta(X_k) \le 19$ costs at least 264. So no admissible partition has cost at most 260 and
$\max_k \ell(X_k) \le 39$: the conclusion of Theorem 4.4 fails for this plan, and no point of
$\mathcal P$ weakly dominates $(260, 39)$.
:::

In that plan, one plane performs the pattern $C_I \to C_4 \to C_3 \to C_I$: it leaves a passenger
in $C_4$ at time 11 and comes back through $C_3$, in $1 + 9 < d_4$, so its pattern lasts
$21 < 2 d_4$, which Lemma 3.4(b) excludes under (H). Under (S) alone, the relaxation $L$ remains a
lower bound for every plan (Lemma 3.5).

In conclusion, we proved that for the Symmetric MultiZenoTravel problem, under the hub triangles
(H), hence under the triangular inequality as well as under the assumption of
[[QS15](#ref-QS15)], every point of the Pareto front is attained by a plan using exactly $2t - p$
central cities, flown from an admissible partition. This will allow a constructive algorithm to
drastically reduce the search space of feasible and Pareto-optimal plans
([Pareto Optimal Plans](#sec-algorithm)).
